businessModel.summary: Rolls-Royce designs and manufactures engines and power systems across three divisions: Civil Aerospace (large engines for wide-body aircraft, with revenue from both engine sales and long-term "TotalCare" maintenance service contracts billed per flying hour), Defence (military aero-engines and systems), and Power Systems (engines/generators for marine, data centre backup, and industrial use).
businessModel.source: Rolls-Royce Holdings plc Annual Report — business overview (https://www.rolls-royce.com/investors.aspx)

competitiveMoat.summary: Wide-body jet engines are a duopoly/triopoly market (Rolls-Royce, GE/CFM, Pratt & Whitney) with very high certification and switching costs; long-life service contracts (installed base of engines already flying) create decades of recurring aftermarket revenue, though programme execution and input cost risk can hurt margins.
competitiveMoat.source: Rolls-Royce Annual Report / public analyst commentary — verify against the latest filing

points: Exceptional cash flow and earnings upgrades: the ongoing business turnaround has delivered strong momentum. Management upgraded its full-year 2026 guidance, expecting underlying operating profit of £4.7bn to £4.9bn and free cash flow reaching £3.8bn to £4.0bn.

Strong structural tailwinds: civil aerospace continues to perform through solid wide-body engine flying hours. Global defense spending remains elevated, while the Power Systems division is capturing profitable growth supplying data centers.

Shareholder returns and credit upgrades: supported by an expanded net cash position, Rolls-Royce re-instituted its dividend with a 6p interim payment and is moving forward with a multi-year £7bn to £9bn share buyback program spanning 2026–2028. Moody's and Fitch also upgraded the company's credit rating to investment grade (A3 and A-, respectively).
Future growth engines: Rolls-Royce's Small Modular Reactors (SMR) nuclear division has succeeded in competitive European tenders, providing long-term high-margin potential.

points: Premium and expensive valuation: despite recent minor retreats and a 20% pullback on macroeconomic and industry headwinds, Rolls-Royce's valuation remains heavily priced for perfection, with a trailing P/E of around 41x.

Risk of earnings disappointment: because the market has grown accustomed to the company smashing expectations, any slight miss or inability to outperform the high end of its raised 2026 operating targets could cause severe volatility.

Aerospace supply chain bottlenecks: the wider aviation sector continues to experience severe supply chain strains. Recent negative supply bottleneck updates from key European aerospace peers like Safran have weighed heavily on investor sentiment.
